Move them straight on to Ex 3B: they read the introduction only, and tell their partner whether anything from their own answer to question 1 is in it. Stop there, the article itself belongs to the next stage.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach the objects by boarding keys, remote, umbrella and so on. That list is the answer to Ex 3B and you will have given it away before they open the book. If a pair dries up on question 1, mime a lost object for them instead.

stages.name: Highlight target language
stages.todo: Set Ex 3C and let them work alone: read the eight numbered tips and match the places (1-8) to the arrows (A-H) in the photo. Four minutes, no checking in pairs. As each student finishes, send them straight into Ex 4A on the same eight tips, finding the eight prepositions of place. Tell them to write down the whole phrase and not the single word, so that you get "under the sofa" and "in front of you" on paper rather than a list of bare prepositions. Keep all the answers back for the next stage.
stages.avoid: Ex 4A prints "Look under the sofa" as its example and six of the eight tips also open with "Look" plus the preposition, so a student can collect most of them without understanding any of them. The two that need real reading are the ones they miss: "near" sits in the middle of tip 7 and "in front of you" is in the second sentence of tip 8. Ask them to write the matching arrow letter beside each phrase, which makes them use the photo to prove it.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Take the Ex 3C matches first with everyone looking at the photo, then build the eight phrases from Ex 4A on the board in the order the article gives them. Meaning comes off the photo and off the room you are standing in: point at a place and ask which phrase it is, and check the two slippery ones by setting them up in front of the class, two cushions for "between" and a student and yourself for "in front of". For form, board the phrase and not the word, show that "next to" and "in front of" are more than one word, and mark that "in front of you" is followed by a person. Finish on Ex 5A and 5B: play 6.01 and let them write the sentences, check what they have, then play it again for the stressed words and get the class saying the sentences with the speakers. Let the recording settle the stress for you rather than deciding it in advance, and use "It's under the bed" from 5B as the sentence you drill.
stages.avoid: If you board the pattern as preposition plus "the" plus noun, the lesson produces "in front of the you" and "between the cushion" within ten minutes. Give "between" two things and keep "in front of you" as its own item on the board.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: The photo beside Ex 5C is your exercise. Working alone, students write one sentence for each arrow A-H, answering the question in 5C's model: "Where's my phone?" "It's under the sofa." One preposition per sentence and no repeats, so all eight get used. They can check themselves against the numbered tips in the article, which name the same eight places in the same room. In the last two minutes put two or three sentences on the board and correct the article and the pronoun, since keys and glasses need "They're between the cushions".
stages.avoid: The eight tips are eight ready-made sentences, so the quickest route for a student is copying "Look under the sofa" eight times. Make the difference explicit: the article gives instructions, you want answers, so every sentence starts "It's" or "They're".

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 7A then 7B, in that order. Three minutes only for the drawing, the furniture and a few of their own things in their favourite room, then pairs show each other the drawings and talk about them. Do it yourself first with a rough room on the board so that they hear where things are and not just a list of nouns. Tell them before they start that you want to hear the eight phrases from the board, and monitor for exactly that. If a pair finishes early, send them back to the exchange in Ex 5C and let them play it on each other's drawings, one asking "Where's my umbrella?" and the other inventing a place. Keep two good sentences and two errors for a short correction slot at the end.
stages.avoid: As printed, "Talk about your room and the furniture" can be passed with "There is a sofa, there is a TV" and not one preposition, so the stage practises nothing unless you set the requirement first and hold them to it.

slots.pages: Speakout A1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 59 (6A)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Get a room and its furniture into the air before anyone has to talk about one. The photo of the room on p.59 does it: ask what the sts can see and collect the words the article is built on, sofa, cushions, shelf, plants, desk, floor, bed, then ask round the class whose room at home looks anything like that one. If you want something more physical, bring your own keys and put them somewhere odd in the room before the lesson and let the class guess where they are. Five minutes is one quick pass, so the words are live rather than taught.
stages.avoid: 3A and 3D are there to open the reading and both point at losing things. A class conversation about lost keys is easy to start and hard to stop, and it feeds nothing into describing a room.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Set 7A: each st draws their favourite room at home with the furniture and the other things in it. Give them a size and a stop, a quick sketch across half a page and no colouring, and tell them what the drawing is for, so they draw things they can actually name. The useful half of this stage is the labelling: as they draw, they write the word next to each thing and put a question mark where they have not got the word. Go round, feed in the nouns they ask for, and note the ones that come up more than once so you can put them up in the next stage.
stages.avoid: Nine minutes is long enough for an A1 class to start shading in the curtains. The drawing is the prompt for 7B, not the product, so do not let neatness become the task and do not correct the drawings.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The article hands you the eight prepositions, under, behind, between, in, next to, on, near and in front of, and each one arrives attached to something concrete, the sofa, the cushions, the box, the plants, the shelf, the floor, the desk. Elicit them rather than reading them out; the photo on p.59 and any st's drawing both give you something to point at, and a CCQ or two will separate behind from next to and in from on better than a definition will. Put the form up in the shape the task needs, It's or They're plus the preposition plus the thing, not in the shape the article prints it in. Model It's under the bed from 5B yourself and drill it, with the stress on under and bed, then show the exchange from 5C, Where's my phone? It's under the sofa, so each st has a question to ask as well as an answer to give. The nouns they asked you for while they were drawing go up here too.
stages.avoid: 4A is a find-the-word task with the answers printed in the same column, so running it as written buys you eight correct answers and no meaning at all. Every one of those eight also sits inside an imperative, Look under the sofa, and sts copy that frame straight into the speaking. 4B then points the class off to the Grammar Bank, which is not part of this slot, and nine minutes in there would turn this into a grammar lesson.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: 7B in pairs: they tell each other about the room, the furniture and where everything is. Give the listener a job or the pair will simply point at the paper, so have the listener draw a rough copy of the room from the description alone, with the drawing kept face down until they have finished, and let them compare the two sketches at the end. That way the prepositions carry the information instead of decorating it. Fifteen minutes is two rounds: run it once, swap the pairs and let them tell a second partner, which is where the fluency actually turns up. Set a floor, five things and where each one is, so the weakest pair knows when it has done enough. Stay out of it while it runs and write down what you hear.
stages.avoid: 7B as printed stops at showing your partner the drawing, and at A1 that ends in nouns and a finger, bed, TV, plant, with no prepositions and nothing for the listener to do. The showing is the part you have to hold back until the room has been described.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content before language: whose room sounds most like their own, which room they would rather sit in, whose copy came out closest to the original drawing. Two or three questions round the class is plenty. Then put up five or six sentences you heard, a mix of ones that worked and ones that did not, with no names on them, and let the class decide which need fixing before you confirm anything. Most of it will be prepositions, and a reformulation on the board will do more here than an explanation. Close with two or three sts saying the corrected sentence aloud.

slots.pages:
Speakout A1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 61 (6B)
Listening: ex. 3a–b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Put two or three questions on the board about where the learners live: what is near your home, what can you walk to from here. A photo of a street, or a rough map of the streets round the school sketched on the board, will carry this at A1 if you can get one. Pairs talk for three minutes while you go round and note the place words they already own. Take two or three answers open class and park the words they gave you in a corner of the board; you add to that corner in the next stage. Say nothing yet about Soraya and Debbie, and set no listening task here.
stages.avoid: There is and there are sit on this page, but they belong to another 6B lesson and this class has not met them. Take what the learners give you as single words and short phrases. Do not reshape their answers into Is there a... ? or There's a... , and do not drill it.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: The recording names shops, a big supermarket, two cafés, a nice Italian restaurant, a very good school, a swimming pool and a park. Only swimming pool sits outside the eight words the lesson after yours teaches, so that one is freely yours; of the rest take two at most and leave the set alone. The words likelier to block this class are not the places at all — area, neighbours and apartment carry the whole situation and come up in the first thirty seconds. Four or five words is the ceiling. Convey the meaning first with a picture, a board drawing or a quick situation, see whether anyone can give you the word before you supply it, check it with one question that does not contain the word, drill it chorally and then by name, and board it with the stress marked. Groups can take a minute first to pool what they already know. Leave the list up; stage four runs off it.
stages.avoid: Do not teach the whole set of places. The next lesson is built on it, and a class that has already met all of it sits through that lesson with nothing to learn. Six minutes also buys you five words done properly or nine done badly, so hold the line at five.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Set Ex 3A before anything is played. Write Soraya and Debbie on the board with the two questions — where are they, and where do they go at the end — and say those two answers are all you want; nothing else goes on paper. Play track 6.02 straight through once. They answer alone, then take it open class: they are neighbours, meeting outside the apartment building they both live in, and at the end they go to Debbie’s flat for a coffee. If the second answer has beaten the room, replay the last few lines rather than the whole track, so the detail stage still has something fresh to offer.
stages.avoid: Do not fade the track out part way through. The second answer is in the closing lines, and a class that never hears the end has nothing to give you. Equally, do not start taking details here because the gist answers come quickly; the room needs a reason to listen again.

stages.name: Listening for specific information and detail
stages.todo: Ex 3B gives you the words listen again, and that is all of it you can use: the task printed beside it points at an exercise on a page this slot does not carry, so the task is yours to build, and the recording gives you everything you need. First, specific information: the words standing on your board from stage two, for the class to tick as they hear them, with two spare lines for other places they catch. Set it, play once, they work alone, check open class — in the area there are shops, a big supermarket, two cafés, an Italian restaurant, a very good school and a park; the swimming pool is the one she asks for that is not there. Then detail, four questions in track order, each answerable in a word or two: how many cafés are there, what kind of restaurant is it, how far away is the swimming pool, and why does Soraya ask about the park. Set them, play again, they answer alone, check open class. If the answers come out thin there is room for one more play before you confirm them.
stages.avoid: Do not read Ex 3B to the class as printed. It sends them to an exercise on a page you have not been given, and you will be improvising a task in front of the class with the recording already cued. Write your own rubric out beforehand and either dictate it or put it on the board.

stages.name: Productive follow-up
stages.todo: Groups of three or four, with their ticked lists and the board words in front of them. Two things to settle: which of the places Soraya and Debbie talked about are also near this school, and which single place each learner would most want near their own home, and why, in whatever English they have. Put a model up in language they already own, for instance we have a park, or I go to the swimming pool. Give them eight minutes and go round collecting what you hear. Each group then reports one thing to the class, and you close on two or three points of correction off your notes.
stages.avoid: Do not slide into the grammar or the writing printed around the listening on this page; both belong to other 6B lessons and are not yours to open. And however naturally the rest of the place words come up here, do not teach them. They are the next lesson's.

slots.pages: Speakout A1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 60 (6B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Sts look at the photos A-C in Ex 1 on p.60 (project them if you can) and you run Ex 1A's two questions in open class: where are these people, and who are they to each other? The page says pairs, but five minutes is not worth the regrouping, so take it from the whole class. Two or three guesses per photo is plenty. If you would rather start closer to home, show a photo of a street the class will recognise and ask the same two questions about it.
stages.avoid: The model exchange printed under Ex 1A hands over 'neighbours', which is one of the three people words Sts are meant to find for themselves in Ex 2A. Read the model if you need it, but do not stop to teach the word here.

stages.name: Noticing the lexis
stages.todo: Set Ex 2A, but have Sts work alone: they read the bullet list in Ex 1B and write two columns, people and places. Nine minutes gives them time to finish and then compare with the person beside them before you take anything in. Then build the two columns on the board from the Sts: three people (friends, family, neighbours) and eight places (supermarket, shops, parks, schools, cinema, sports centre, restaurants, cafés). Leave the board up, because those eight are what you work on next.
stages.avoid: Ex 2A prints the first answer in each column for you, 'people: friends' and 'places: supermarket', so a St can copy those two and look finished. Tell the class the two examples are free and you want the other nine words, or cover them.

stages.name: MPF clarification
stages.todo: Work through the eight places on the board one at a time, meaning before the word: a quick sketch, what you buy or do there, or a point out of the window if the thing is round the corner, and let the Sts hand you the word. Then take form and pronunciation together while each word is still live, so plurals (shops, parks, cafés), the stress on SPORTS centre, and the ending on café (/ˈkæfeɪ/). Drill the three or four the class finds hardest in chorus and then one or two Sts on their own. Ex 2B asks what other places Sts know, so if they offer any, put two or three on the board and move on; you have nine minutes and eight words to get through.
stages.avoid: The page prints the words inside phrases, 'a good supermarket and other shops' and 'a cinema and a sports centre', so Sts take the whole chunk to be the item. Pull the single word out each time. Ex 2B also tells Sts to check in the Vocabulary Bank, which is not on your card, so keep that check in the room.

stages.name: Practice and production
stages.todo: Give the words a run before Sts have to use them for real: two or three minutes in pairs with the Ex 1B list covered, rebuilding the eight places from memory, then they uncover and check against the page. Then run Ex 1B itself with something to settle, so each pair has to agree on the three things that matter most where they live and be ready to name the one they could not live without. Monitor and write down what you hear. Swap two or three pairs if they dry up, and if a pair finishes early ask them whether their three would be the same for someone much older.
stages.avoid: Ex 1B looks like a discussion but at this level it collapses into reading the bullets aloud, which is why the pairs need the agreement and the one thing they could not live without. The words also sit next to the there is, there are section of the page, so do not ask for sentences in that grammar: it has not been taught.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two halves, and watch the clock. Content first: ask three or four pairs for their top three and see where the class lands, with a show of hands on the one thing nobody could live without. Then language: put five or six things you heard during Ex 1B on the board, correct and incorrect mixed together, and let the class sort them before you confirm anything. Make at least two of them pronunciation, word stress or the ending on cafés, because that is where these words go first. Close by drilling whichever ones needed it once more.

slots.pages: Speakout A1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 61 (6B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Get sts talking about the places around this school. Bring in or show a photo of one street nearby and ask what you can find on it and what is missing. Stay on the places themselves (shops, a cafe, a school, a park, a swimming pool) so that the words the task needs are already in the air before anyone chooses a role. Five minutes is two or three questions and a few short answers, not a discussion.
stages.avoid: The writing section on your page is tempting as a warmer text. Ex 7A sends sts to read the opening of the post about Ealing and write questions about it, and only the first lines of that post are on your page. Read it here and your five-minute lead-in becomes a reading stage with nowhere to go.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Decide your pairs before this stage starts and let each pair settle on one role from step 1 of the 6B box, so the two of them prepare the same town: a family with two young children, a young couple with a dog, retired people, or young single businesspeople. Then step 2 on their own and in silence, each st listing the six places that matter to that role with a reason for each, following the book's example, a school is important for our children. Leave step 3, the diagram, for the pair stage, because they need someone to disagree with. Nine minutes alone is a long time at A1, so give them the number six as a target and monitor to catch anyone who has stopped.
stages.avoid: Two of the four roles carry words your sts may not have at this level, retired and businesspeople. Check those are understood before anyone picks, or you will spend the speaking task explaining a role instead of listening to the language.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 4A carries the language the task runs on. Clarify there's and there are for the statements, Is there a...? and Are there any...? for the questions, and the short answers from the example exchange under 5C, yes, there is, there's a post office ten minutes from me. Add the two moves printed in the box, why is that important? and it's important because..., since the pairs cannot argue about the diagram without them. Take 5A's linking in by voice, drilling there's a and are there any as if each were one word, rather than building the stage round the recording. Board only what they will say in the next fifteen minutes.
stages.avoid: Do not set 4A as a written gap-fill to be checked. Its first answer is already printed in full in 5A, are there any shops near here?, and yes, there is sits in the example under 5C, so the exercise tests nothing. Use those sentences as your models and keep this a clarification stage, not a grammar lesson.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 6A, run through steps 3 and 4 of the box. Pairs copy the two rings from the diagram, near home, you can walk, and 3-4 kilometres from home, into their notebooks, then place their six places and put family and friends in as well. The book gives them the moves for it, what things can we put near home?, I think a supermarket is important, why is that important?, so insist that nothing goes into a ring until both of them have said why. Give the diagram about eight minutes, then re-pair sts with someone from another pair for the telling round in 6B and the comparison in 6C, which the book sets for groups, and which a new pair does just as well with the card you have. Monitor without joining in and write down what you hear for the last stage.
stages.avoid: A diagram task can go quiet, with sts drawing and writing instead of speaking. There is nothing to hand out here, so the drawing is theirs to do in a notebook from the book's picture, and it should take seconds. If you see tidy circles and silence, stop and give the pair a question to answer out loud.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first. Take 6C's two questions to the whole class, what do you like about each town and is anything the same in all the diagrams, and get two or three sts to say which town they would rather live in and why. Then put five or six things you heard on the board, a mix of accurate and inaccurate there is and there are, plus a link or two that fell apart, and let sts sort and repair them before you confirm anything. Keep the content half to about three minutes so the correction half actually happens.
